   Whether you choose some sort of exercise or playing a musical in-
strument or a period of study, the key to making progress is the consis-

Think Big but Start Small
I believe that a major reason why people fail to create the habits they
want is because they try to go too big. For example, we decide we are
going to exercise for an hour a day when we haven’t exercised in years.
Or we try to go from not watching any training videos to watching and
taking notes on three hours of training videos a day. Our attempts usually
backfire because we over-estimate how much motivation we have and,
as already discussed, installing new habits is uncomfortable for the first
few weeks. By trying to do too much, we increase the likelihood of failing,
which then de-motivates us and keeps us stuck right where we are. As a
side note, it is advisable to tackle one habit change at a time. After you
get one installed and on autopilot, you can move on to the next one.
Don’t try to change everything at once! Finally, if you are a procrastinator,
going small will often work, because the tasks are so small that they will
elicit minimal resistance.
    Stephen Guise, author of Mini Habits, gives two compelling reasons for
going small: doing a little is infinitely bigger and better than doing nothing,
and doing a little bit every day has a greater impact than doing a lot on
just one day. This is because a little bit each day is much more likely to
grow into a lifelong habit. B. J. Fogg, director of the Persuasive Technol-
ogy Lab at Stanford University, studies how behavior works, and he advo-
cates creating tiny habits for creating positive behaviors. He suggests
three steps for building a tiny habit:

                                                    Create Winning Habits

   ♠ Go ridiculously small. Pick a very small step towards your goal. He
       gives an example of a person who wants to build a habit of flossing
       their teeth. His advice: floss one tooth per day. Guise ultimately
       wanted to do 100 push-ups per day, but his mini habit was one
       push-up a day. Because these steps are so small, you are much
       more likely to complete the behavior – even if you feel unmo-
       tivated. Meeting your goal with 100% success creates a positive
       feedback loop, which will increase your self-efficacy and make it
       more likely that you will do more than the minimum requirement.
       You are building a routine, and there’s no possible way that doing
       one repeat of an exercise can be threatening. On the off chance
       that it is, you can go to the gym, walk in, and then immediately turn
       around and leave. Continue in that vein until going to the gym is a
       routine, and then add your one rep or one minute on the treadmill.
       You can adapt this system however you like. The only requirement
       is that you make your habits too small to fail. Consistency is what
       you are really after, and going small ensures you’ll be consistent.
   ♠ Find an anchor. Choose some existing activity in your life to act as
       a trigger for your new behavior. Whether you realize it or not,
       there are lots of behaviors you already do habitually, like brushing
       your teeth or taking a shower. Take one of your routines and
       connect it to your tiny new behavior. To add more exercise to
       your day, for example, you may decide that after you brush your
       teeth, you will do one push-up.
   ♠ Reward yourself immediately. Fogg says that it is important to
       reward yourself in small ways as soon as you complete your new
       tiny habit. An “atta boy” or a thumbs up will do the trick. The key is
       to reinforce desired behavior. This helps you build success
       momentum.

   Fogg’s research has shown that building tiny habits has profound ripple
effects. People who try it feel more confident about their ability to create
more good habits in the future, and as many as 65% report that it led

Peak Poker Performance

them to make additional positive changes. Thus, tiny habits have a New-
tonian effect: for most people just getting started on new behaviors is
difficult, but once they are in motion, it is often easy to just keep going.

Identify Your Kryptonite
As you look at your lifestyle to determine what habits will enhance your
performance, also take the time to look at which habits have the biggest
negative impact on you. There is a saying that you should pull out the
weeds before you plant the flowers: you have to get rid of whatever is
not serving you well before you can bring in the good stuff. If you don’t,
the weeds will quickly overrun your beautiful flowers.
   Everyone has their version of kryptonite. Make a commitment to stop
doing whatever it is that brings you down. Determine that you will never
do this behavior again. If you slip up, that’s alright. Just get back up and
start again. Don’t beat yourself up. It’s important to have self-
compassion. Changing habits is hard, but it is worth the effort.

Embrace the Process
Peak performance is earned through a very long process of hard work. It
may take years to design your behavior for mastery. The most important
trait to possess is grit, which is a combination of intense passion and in-
tense persistence, and one of the most powerful predictors of success.
Gritty people simply don’t give up.
    You also want to embrace what is known as a growth mindset. When-
ever your results are not to your liking, approach the situation as a scien-
tist would. A scientist merely gathers data. Failure is not seen as a “bad”
thing. Rather it is information that is used to make adjustments. Have no
emotional attachment to whatever results you get. Instead think about
how you can use the data to refine your process. Simply ask, “How can I
improve?”

                                                  Create Winning Habits

Summary
As you can see from the information in this chapter, the difference be-
tween success and failure often comes down to habits. If you have been
less successful than you would like, start by asking yourself what small
changes you can make to progress towards your goals. Think about what
one thing you could either start or stop doing that would increase your
chances of success, then work to make that into a habit. Here are a few
tips for building habits in the most efficient manner possible:

   ♠ Be 100% committed. We must be fully committed to our new
       good habit. Shut down that whiny little voice in your head that
       tries to talk you into taking a day off. It’s easy to fall prey to
       thoughts of quitting. If you are not committed, you’ll come up with
       excuses (e.g. too tired, too busy, etc.). Make it non-negotiable.
       We produce change when we’re all-in! You can’t make that level
       of commitment to 10 habits at once. Pick one that you’ll
       absolutely crush. Your good habit needs to be non-negotiable. Go
       all-in on your most important keystone habit.
   ♠ Make it a daily habit. That’s the only way to really create
       momentum. If we skip days, it becomes easier to skip more, and
       that’s how habits fall apart. Consistent action is the key to
       success. What’s your daily goal? What will you do every single
       day?
   ♠ Make it easy to win. If you are currently not exercising, don’t try
       to exercise for 60 minutes. Try for 1 minute or 5 minutes. Create
       a series of wins which you can build on later. Track your wins, and
       do not break the streak. A series of tiny wins is the precursor to
       big change.
   ♠ If you miss a day, definitely don’t miss two! I got this idea from a
       book called Superhuman by Habit by Tynan. He says if you miss a
       day, schedule it in for the next day, and make it the number one
       thing you do. Don’t beat yourself up; just get back on track.

     ♠ Make bright lines. It’s easier to do something when you are 100%
        committed to it. It has to be clear. Saying “I’ll drink less” is not
        clear. A true bright line is “I’ll never drink again.” You know when
        you are approaching your bright line, and you certainly know when
        you have crossed it.
     ♠ Create a stop-doing list. You have to pull out the weeds before
        you plant the flowers. What bad habits do you need to remove?
        What can you replace it with? Crowd out your negative habits
        with new positive habits. What’s bringing you down? Make it hard
        to do your bad habits and easy to do your good ones.


Chapter Highlights
     ♠ Making habits and breaking habits is a critical part of the peak
        performance process.
     ♠ Use less willpower by making as many good behaviors as possible
        into habits.
     ♠ Building habits is easier if you are 100% committed.
     ♠ Small habits are easier to make and keep than complex ones.
     ♠ Exercise, sleep, and eating well are keystone habits that can be the
        foundation for other good habits.
     ♠ Mastery is a long-term process that requires the right mindset.

                                                   Create Winning Habits

fast and lunch option to eat while traveling the poker circuit. I was
prompted to find a healthy option because most casinos offer primarily
unhealthy food, plus having to spend an hour of my morning finding food
seemed like a poor use of time. So, I started drinking large quantities of
blended vegetables. These smoothies take about five minutes to make,
drink, and clean up, which frees up lots of extra time to sleep and relax.
They are also incredibly healthy, especially compared with pancakes and
waffles. For lunch, I frequently blend one up in the morning and throw it in
my backpack. The smoothies take a bit of planning to have on the poker
circuit, as I have to pack a blender and buy groceries before my trip, but I
think the health benefits and time saved are well worth the effort.
    Another habit I recently implemented is waking up a few hours before
the tournament and spending some time relaxing and getting in a great
state of mind. In the past, I would play poker until 1am, sleep until 11am,
roll out of bed, and then play my daily tournament at noon. While I maxi-
mized the number of hours played each day, I was generally unhappy and
almost certainly wasn’t in my best state of mind. Now, I try to get back in
my room before 11pm and I try to wake up before 10am. This gives me a
bit of time to work out, read books, meditate, and enjoy life. I have found
that when I am not rushed and have a few hours to spend doing exactly
what I want, I think more clearly at the poker table, which allows me to
make better decisions.
    One habit I have been working hard to break is one where I go out and
have a few too many drinks after a rough day at the poker tables. If you
stroll through the casino near the end of the day, you will almost certainly
see many poker players drinking their bad beats away. While their actions
probably aren’t too detrimental, especially if they are disciplined enough
to only have a few drinks and get to sleep relatively early, they likely have
negative effects. Given I want to spend my mornings relaxing, I do not
see how nights out partying are beneficial for me. The habit of going out
and having a drink is quite difficult for most people to break. I have found
that instead of going out at night, or even keeping alcohol in my hotel
